questions.q: A forecasting model uses a **centred** 7-day rolling mean of sales (3 days before, the day itself and 3 days after) as a feature. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; rolling means are standard features
Centred windows are too short
Look-ahead leakage: the feature uses future sales that would not be known at forecast time, so backtest results will look better than reality
Rolling means are only allowed for monthly data
questions.why: Ask of every input: would I have known this exact value when the forecast had to be made? A centred window peeks 3 days ahead. Use a trailing window that ends at the forecast origin.

questions.q: A retailer needs forecasts **8 weeks ahead** to place orders. At what horizon should the model be tested?
options: 1 week ahead, because it is the most accurate
Any horizon; accuracy does not depend on it
8 weeks ahead, the horizon the business decision actually needs
On the training data, at no horizon
questions.why: Errors usually grow with the horizon, so a model tested 1 week ahead will look far better than it performs at 8 weeks. Test at the horizon the decision uses.

questions.q: Four SKUs have actuals 50, 200, 150, 100 and forecasts 60, 180, 165, 100. What is the WAPE?
questions.why: Absolute errors: 10, 20, 15, 0, total 45. WAPE = total absolute error / total actual = 45 / 500 = 9.0%. 10.0% is the MAPE (average of 20%, 10%, 10%, 0%); 11.25 is the MAE in units; 1.0% is the bias, where over- and under-forecasts cancel.

questions.q: Forecast errors on four periods are 2, 2, 2 and 14 units. What are the MAE and RMSE?
options: MAE 5.0, RMSE 7.2
MAE 5.0, RMSE 5.0
MAE 7.2, RMSE 5.0
MAE 5.0, RMSE 52.0
questions.why: MAE = 20 / 4 = 5.0. RMSE = √((4 + 4 + 4 + 196) / 4) = √52 ≈ 7.2. RMSE squares errors before averaging, so the single large miss counts much more. 52 is the mean squared error before taking the square root.

questions.q: A demand model has **MASE = 1.25** on the backtest. What does that mean?
options: The model's errors are 25% smaller than a naive forecast's
The model's average error is 25% larger than a naive forecast's typical error on the history; the simple "same as last time" rule would do better
The model has 125% accuracy
The model is 1.25 units off on average
questions.why: MASE divides the model's MAE by the naive forecast's MAE on the training data. Below 1 is better than naive; above 1 is worse. It is scale-free, so it is not in units.

questions.q: A product range includes several slow sellers that sometimes sell zero units in a week. Why is MAPE a poor headline metric here?
options: MAPE ignores large errors
MAPE cannot be computed for weekly data
MAPE is always lower than WAPE
MAPE divides by each actual, so small actuals produce huge percentages and zero actuals make it undefined; WAPE or MASE is more stable
questions.why: One SKU with actual 10 and forecast 20 adds a 100% error that can dominate MAPE. WAPE weights by volume and MASE scales by a naive benchmark, so neither blows up. MAPE is often higher than WAPE for exactly this reason.

questions.q: Last week's sales only become final each Wednesday, so forecasts made on Monday cannot use them. How should the backtest reflect this?
options: Ignore it; the effect is small
Leave a gap between the training and test periods (for example the `gap` parameter in `TimeSeriesSplit`) so the model only sees data that would have been available
Shuffle the data so the delay averages out
Use random k-fold cross-validation
questions.why: The backtest must mimic real information flow. A gap stops the model using data that would not yet be final, which is a subtle form of look-ahead leakage. Shuffling or random k-fold makes the leakage worse.

questions.q: In an interview: "Your demand model scored 4% MAPE on a random 20% hold-out, but in production its error is about 15%. What probably went wrong?"
options: Production data is always noisier, so nothing went wrong
MAPE should have been replaced with RMSE
The model needs more parameters

The random split let the model train on future data and test on interleaved past points (plus likely leaky features), so the hold-out was not an honest forecast test; re-evaluate with a rolling-origin backtest at the business horizon and compare with a naive baseline
questions.why: Random splits break time order: neighbouring days end up on both sides, so the model effectively interpolates. A rolling-origin backtest trains only on the past, tests on the future, and shows how the error varies across windows. Changing the metric does not fix a leaky design.
